title: Passover: as if you left (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5)
hook: in every generation each person must see themselves as if they left Egypt

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dayenu, fifteen gifts counted one by one. Your line was it would have been enough. Did you write down three? Today, the line that makes the whole seder personal. Day six hundred eighty-one.

An anniversary looks back. A wedding anniversary remembers a day that happened to two people. A national holiday remembers founders who are long gone. You honor them, but you weren't there. The seder could easily work the same way: here's what happened to our ancestors, long ago, pass the matzah. But there's a sentence in the Mishnah, read aloud at the seder, that refuses to let the story stay in the past tense. It doesn't ask you to remember the Exodus. It asks for something much stranger.
screen: `ANNIVERSARIES LOOK BACK.` → `YOU WEREN'T THERE.` → `A SENTENCE THAT REFUSES.`

segments.voice: The Mishnah, at the end of the tractate on Passover, first gives Rabban Gamliel's rule: anyone who hasn't explained three things at the seder, the Passover offering, matzah and bitter herbs, hasn't fulfilled the duty of the night. Then it says: in every generation, a person is obligated to see himself as if he himself came out of Egypt. Not our ancestors. Me. And it proves it with the verse we met two days ago, in the old Jewish translation: "It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt." For me. When I came out. The verse speaks in the first person to people who were never slaves. Maimonides, in his version of this law, uses a slightly different word: a person must show himself as if he left. Show, not just see. That's why, he says, people recline at the seder, like free people at a banquet, and drink the cups. The body acts it out. And the Mishnah draws a conclusion. Because we came out, it says, we're obligated to thank and praise God. Then the seder breaks into the Psalms of praise. So remembering turns into gratitude, and gratitude into song. There's one more layer, a wordplay Hasidic teachers used. The Hebrew name for Egypt, Mitzrayim, sounds like meitzarim: narrow places, tight straits. So every person, they taught, has an Egypt: a narrow place they've been held. The seder asks each one to stand in the doorway of their own leaving, every year.
screen: `RABBAN GAMLIEL'S THREE THINGS.` · `IN EVERY GENERATION, AS IF YOU.` · `SEE IT, AND SHOW IT.` · `MITZRAYIM: THE NARROW PLACE.` · then, large: `AS IF YOU LEFT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: imagine leaving a narrow place. Sit back, the way someone free would sit. Breathe. Think of a narrow place you've been in: a job, an illness, a fear, a relationship, a season of your life when the walls felt close. Now picture the moment you stepped out, or the step you hope to take. Feel your shoulders open. You don't have to be fully out. Just stand in the doorway for a moment, as if you left. The bell holds the time.
Passover. The festival of leaving Egypt, told in the first person, as if you yourself left. Today's word.
Your line: as if you left. Today, tell one part of your story in the present tense, as if it's still yours to walk through. Day six hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: At the seder, the Haggadah reads the Mishnah's line that in every generation each person must see themselves as if they left Egypt; people recline and drink four cups as free people, and then sing the Psalms of Hallel.

trapdoor: what you thought: the seder remembers what happened long ago.
what it means: each person tells it as if they themselves left, and then gives thanks.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Pesachim 10:5 builds on Exodus 13:8's 'for me'; Maimonides' code reads 'to show himself', tying it to reclining and the cups.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut "three thousand years" (voice and fork) and the "most anniversaries" / "every seder" claims; the Mitzrayim wordplay is now framed as one Hasidic teachers used.
Exodus 13:8 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory (same quotation as day 679); verify.
Mishnah Pesachim 10:5 paraphrased: Rabban Gamliel's three things; 'in every generation'; 'therefore we are obligated to thank...'. Verify.
Maimonides, Chametz u-Matzah 7:6–7: 'lehar'ot et atzmo' (to show himself), with reclining. Verify reference.
Mitzrayim / meitzarim is a homiletical play, labeled as a Hasidic teaching, not an etymology.
